title: Shall We Begin?
mood: The frontline fights as one at last, until the storm over the Academy comes down.

hero.alt: A cat-eared drone flies past a broken bridge and the view drops to a ruined street, where blue arcs cut through the Enders and Vexana in her robe blasts them with violet light; then a purple-and-gold giant with a sword cuts through the Enders below a rooftop.

segs.t: Fanny came down off the platforms with both blades out and rain in her face. The rig at her hips roared.
Below her, Enders were still dropping out of the small black ships. They landed on roofs and in doorways. One hit the bay road ahead of her and split the stones.
“Frontline,” said Lesley on the channel. “Your ground is the Academy district. Below the hill, from the bay road up to the hall. The shelters at your back are full. Rear support, stay close behind.”
“Understood,” said Fanny.
She took the bay road at roof height. Her cable shot out, caught a lamppost and swung her round it into an Ender’s back. Blade. A kick of the thrusters. The next one.
The wind tore at her hair. Once she had told a little girl on her hip that flying felt great. It still did. She was grinning, and for once the Shield part of her let it be.
Ahead, Guinevere flew on wings of gold light, her two drones circling her. Their yellow rings blazed.
“Left, the big one,” Guinevere told her drones. “Right, stop showing off.”
The right drone cracked an Ender across the head anyway. The Ender swung at it, and its chest plates split. Guinevere laughed and put her fist into the core.

Vexana flew beside her on wings of violet. She lifted her free hand. Her three giants came down off the platforms behind her and landed in the road. Their swords fell together. The stones burst, and light ran out along the road and knocked the Enders flat.
Fanny’s eyes stayed on the giants a moment too long. Then she found her next Ender.

On a roof over the road Layla knelt with the cannon on her shoulder. The cyan cells on its stock filled one after another, and her lips moved with them. She fired. At the end of the road something tall fell over.

Behind them rose the bay road cut, a narrow street that climbed from the water to the shelters. At its top Angela held her shield over a knot of wounded soldiers. Its pink light curved down around them on every side. She held it with both hands and talked to the men under it the whole time. Ruby walked its edge, her scythe crackling.
Guinevere dropped beside Vexana at the mouth of the cut. At her collar the small gold star was lit. Through Vexana’s sleeve, at the wrist, a second star glowed with it.
Guinevere looked back at Fanny, then up at Layla’s roof. Her fists came up.
“We have only one Aspirant spirit.”
The four of them went in together.
An Ender stepped out of a doorway behind Vexana, on her left, where she was not looking. Its arm went up. Its chest plates began to split.
For one beat Fanny’s blades did not move. Vexana wore an Ender’s robe and carried an Ender’s staff.
Cover her,
Fanny told herself, the way she would have told a squad.
She dropped between them. Her blade went into the open chest as the claw came down. The Ender burst apart over Vexana’s shoulder.
Vexana looked back and nodded, once.
Fanny turned to the next one. She left her back to Vexana.
On her roof Layla was grinning.
“And now, it’s our time to shine!”
“Hey,” said Fanny. “That’s my line!”
Guinevere laughed out loud, and her drones bobbed with her.
“The landings have stopped,” said Chang’e on the channel. “Every reading on my board is still going up. You’re pushing them back to the water.”
For a moment the bay road was nearly clear. Fanny hung over it, breathing hard. Rain ran off her blades.
Then the storm overhead came down.
Its black cloud had spread over the hill behind them. Now the cloud sank, and the Storm Citadel came down out of it.
Fanny had watched it come through the mouth from the platforms. Once, in Joe’s class, she had seen it in a shaking film. Neither had shown her how big it was close up.
It filled the sky over the Academy, from the hill to the water. Under it the bell tower looked small.
In the old record, every machine under its storm had died. Fanny felt for her rig. It was still humming.
The Storm Citadel.
In her throne hall, Obsidia looked down. Through the eyes of her Enders the street lay under her, and every Aspirant in it was burning bright.
Her storm hung over the city and struck at nothing. The spine could not feed the storm and the field at once.
“Shall we begin?” she said.
She opened her hands. Over each palm a small black sphere woke, ringed with fire. She laid them against the throne behind her, and a new hum ran down the spine into every block.

media.alt: Obsidia, close, holds out her clawed hands; over each floats a small black sphere ringed with fire.

segs.t: The Academy district.
A second hum came down from the ship, deeper than its own. Fanny felt it in her chest before she heard it.
Vexana had stopped in the air. Her hand went to her jaw.
“I know that hum,” she said. Then, louder: “Land. All of you. Now.”
“Why?” said Fanny.
Vexana did not answer. She was already dropping toward the road.
Rubble began to rise off the road. Chips of curb first. Then slabs of paving, and stones the size of vans, lifting slowly into the air and hanging there, turning.
Under the ship a light swelled. It was a sphere, magenta, and its edge crawled with flickering squares. It took in the hall’s roofs, then the streets below them, and kept coming.
“Fanny?” said Layla. “What is that?”
Fanny had no answer. Vexana had known it was coming.
“Frontline, land!” she called on the channel, and tipped her thrusters at the road.
The edge reached the top of the cut first.
Angela’s shield flickered over the wounded and went out. The men under it looked up. Angela stood with her hands still raised, holding nothing.
“Is this the end?” Angela whispered on the channel.
The edge rolled over Layla’s roof. She pulled the trigger, and the cannon gave nothing. Its cyan cells went dark one after another, counting the wrong way. Her voice came over the channel.
“Huh...? No way... What...”
Then it reached Fanny. She was still two stories up.
The rig at her hips coughed once and went silent. Her cable went slack and dark. The wind kept going, and she dropped out of it.
She hit the road shoulder first and rolled. She came up on one knee with grit in her teeth.
Above her the edge went on toward the water.
Vexana was near the road. Her violet wings folded into nothing, and she dropped the last few meters onto the road, on her feet.
Beside her a giant was in mid-swing. Its yellow eyes went out. Its sword came down by its own weight, struck the stones and lay there. Behind it the other two had stopped where they stood.
Guinevere had been the farthest out, over the water. At Fanny’s call she turned and saw Vexana on the road. She came flying back to her, high and fast, not down.
The edge took her last.
Her drones’ yellow rings went out. They tipped over and dropped out of the sky. Her gold wings broke apart into sparks, and Guinevere fell after them.
She came down through a shop’s awning and hit the stones at the mouth of the cut. She did not get up.
Then the street was quiet. No rig hummed. No drone whined. Along the bay road the lamps still burned. Out on the bay the rain hissed on the water.

media.alt: A wall of magenta light sweeps down a dark street; Guinevere, flying on wings of fire with her two drones, is caught in it, her wings break into flickering squares and the drones go dim and fall; then she crashes onto the stones and lies among her dark drones.

segs.t: Vexana was already running. Fanny ran too. Her legs still worked.
Guinevere lay on her side with her eyes open, one arm pressed against her ribs. Vexana knelt over her and said her name. Guinevere’s eyes found her.
One of her drones lay beside her, gray, its ring dark. Her fingers had found its ear. It was the right one.
Fanny dropped to one knee on her other side. At Guinevere’s collar the gold star was dark. Through Vexana’s sleeve nothing shone at all.
On the platform Fanny had heard those two stars answer each other. She looked from one to the other. Neither gave any light.
She looked down at her own blades. The cyan had gone from their edges. They were steel, and nothing more.
One weapon still had its light. At the top of the cut Ruby’s scythe crackled on. Fanny did not know why.
The channel still worked too.
“Comms hold,” said Lesley. “Suits don’t. It isn’t the storm from the records.”
Layla came down off her roof by the drainpipe, the dead cannon slung on her back. She stopped at Fanny’s left and said nothing.
Over the road the stones hung, turning.
Down by the water the Enders came on out of the smoke. They walked. They were in no hurry now.
Up the cut, in a shelter doorway, a small boy was crying.
Soldiers hold ground with no suits at all,
Fanny thought.
Two years I watched them do it.
She got to her feet. She set them the way the soldiers had taught her, and raised two blades of plain steel.
“As humanity’s last hope, I can’t afford to give up.”
